summary: A Network Host Status report covering May 8 to May 19, 1972. Testing was skipped on May 15 because of the attempt to install the new IMP system. The MIT-AI and Stanford PDP-10 hosts each became network servers. It was replaced by RFC 353.

eli5.summary: This is like a school attendance sheet for the early internet. Someone wrote down which big computers were switched on and ready to help, and which ones were not, so people knew where to go.

questions: when did mit and stanford join arpanet
subtitle: Checking which network hosts were working in May 1972

tldr.problem: Users needed current information on which ARPANET hosts were functioning and available for use.
tldr.mechanism: BBN tested network hosts from May 8 to May 19, 1972. MIT-AI and Stanford became network servers during this period. Testing was skipped on May 15 due to IMP system installation.
tldr.outcome: The report showed growing network availability. Major research institutions like MIT and Stanford became operational servers.

today: RFC 353 replaced this status report in June 1972. MIT and Stanford remained key parts of the ARPANET for decades.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: RFC 344 reports on host status from May 8 to May 19, 1972. During this interval, both the MIT Artificial Intelligence Group PDP-10 (Address 134) and the Stanford PDP-10 (Address 11) each became network servers, representing significant growth of operational resources on the ARPANET. Testing was not conducted on May 15 due to an attempt to install the new IMP system.
sections.eli5: Two major computer science research centers, MIT and Stanford, had their computers become available for other sites to use. Someone was also trying to upgrade the network's main switching system.

sections.title: Host Categories
sections.content:
By May 1972, most hosts excluded from daily testing fell into two categories: user-only hosts (Terminal IMPs at AMES, MITRE, NBS, ETAC, USC, GWC, and BBN) and the Network Control Center (Address 5) which gathered statistics. Only one non-server host remained excluded: the PDP-10 at Case, expected to begin serving in June.

The operational server network now included UCLA, SRI, UCSB, UTAH, MIT-Multics, MIT-AI, RAND, SDC, Harvard, Lincoln, Stanford, Carnegie, and AMES. This represented the core of the early ARPANET's shared computing resources.
sections.eli5: The network had grown to the point where most big computer centers were either running as servers or waiting to start. Only a few machines were still just receiving data.

sections.title: Status and Reliability
sections.content:
The status tables show that Open (O) and Dead (D) statuses dominated the results. Most servers achieved multiple Open states across the testing period, though issues persisted. Some machines like SRI-AI remained consistently dead, while Half Open (H) states indicated connection problems on new servers like MIT-AI.

The addition of MIT-AI as a server showed immediate connection difficulties (mostly H status), typical of newly connected systems. Stanford performed more reliably despite being a new server. The network's infrastructure remained challenged, with many hosts experiencing periodic unavailability.
sections.eli5: Some computers were very reliable and often answered connections (O). Others were broken or unreachable (D). New computers sometimes had trouble connecting at first, which was normal when starting out.
